utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: We used to have it when we were members of the operational units of the JNA. They were distributed by the organ for morale in the unit command. Practically every soldier had received a booklet like that. We were also trained on the international laws of war, as was every other soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the passage of convoys through VRS-controlled area along the Pale-Lukavica road. Please tell the Chamber which road exactly was used by humanitarian convoys to move from Pale?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The humanitarian convoys from Pale went via Trebevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene, but I was just wondering if we could have the paragraph numbers as we're going along, just so we could follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us where this is found in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 25, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one which bears the number 1D -- now it is 532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if it would be called up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have it in e-court then. D532, paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any suggestion that it could be paragraph 26 or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That is precisely why we applied for this statement to be admitted, because it corresponds with the previous evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree that I'm still suffering from the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just request going forward. I see from the previous question actually a fact was inserted that's not in the statement. I'd just -- if we could watch the leading on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you've heard the request which seems to be a reasonable request by Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Can we then have paragraph 14 of the D533 statement in parallel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please provide us with an answer to the best of your recollection in terms of what route was used by such humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: If they went from Gorazde, they went through Pale along the Trebevic road, which we controlled up to Vrace. And then from Vrace, across the Vrbanja bridge and onto federation territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At some point you said that in April 1995, you personally received an order from General Mladic. Please tell the Court about it.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic called us in April, and I happened to be the duty operations officer. He wanted to speak to the commander who was absent. He then told me, "Listen carefully, tell this to the commander and Cedo Sladoje, who was Chief of Staff, they should be very careful with the arrival of Gorazde and Zepa wounded. They were to go through your area of responsibility and nothing should happen to them. Provide a safe passage. And if you have, give them some oranges too. Do bear this in mind and pass it on to the other commanders." He asked me if it was clear, and I said yes. I conveyed that order to the commanders and to the staff units in order to ensure that safe passage of the convoy through our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I have a little concern here. Your questions to the witness elicit the information that is already on D533. So while we have the explanations in D533, you're still repeating them orally. It does look like we're not going to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will conclude with the next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, which were the specific ways you used in order to establish that artillery was being used from the compound of the Kosevo hospital to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: We could see it from the our observation points, and each soldier of ours could observe it. And there was a -- a dedicated soldier in every platoon and company to observe. That task was also issued to each and every soldier, not only to man their positions but to observe as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: By doing so, did you have the occasion to see whether the BH Army also used tanks in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had a tank which they kept hidden in the tunnel underneath Kosevo hill through which one could reach Velesici. They would come out and then go back, opening fire occasionally. They also engaged our forward command post at Vrace. It was destroyed. And I even happened to find myself under a pile of rocks in the process on the 8th of June, 1992. Several people died when we were targeted by their tank. Some soldiers, as well as my signalsman, who lost his leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I thank you for your answers. I hand you over to the Prosecution and would kindly ask you to provide answers to them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before inviting Mr. Weber to proceed, could you tell us about the Kosevo hospital artillery firing. How often did you observe artillery being fired from the Kosevo hospital compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On several occasions. Especially in the evening, because you could see the flame from the nozzle, and my soldiers called me to see. It was a mobile artillery group with pieces mounted on the TAM trucks. They would fire and then move on to another position, provoking us to engage the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you say on several occasions, was that four times a year, was it five times a week, was it -- could you tell us a bit more in detail what the frequency was? Because that was what my question was about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several times. Because their artillery was mobile. It was several times. I would say over a hundred during the four years while I was there. They always used one route, opened fire, and moved on to another, opening fire again. They would go to Bascarsija, and then to Kosevo, in order to open fire. So we couldn't engage them with our artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is, on average, at least 25 times a year. That's every second week, once. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, roughly. Yes. I cannot say very precisely. It's not that I took notes every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Veljovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Today my initial questions will relate to your military career and assignments between 1991 and 1995. In your statement, which is admitted as D532, you indicate that you were part of the 216th JNA Mountain Brigade starting on 30 June 1991. Is it correct that Dragomir Milosevic was the commander of the 216th Brigade when you joined?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the brigade considerably before Dragomir Milosevic. In -- he joined it only in 1989, whereas I joined it only in 1997 [as interpreted]. And it's true that we were mobilised in June 1991, and I was already there as the assistant commander for operations and teaching because the current General Ganic -- actually, at that time, he was the chief for -- chief of operations for the 216th Brigade, and I was the desk officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I think you should --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- clarify the dates --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- at the beginning of this answer. But it would be helpful if you could indicate as well to which paragraph of that statement you are referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe it's paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of the current version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in your answer, you were just recorded as stating that General Milosevic joined in 1989, whereas you joined only in 1997. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. I was deployed in the command of that brigade in 1997 when I completed the school for reserve officers and when I got out of school. And I stayed on until the 19th of May, 1992 in the 216th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please listen carefully. Is it correct that you joined the 216th Mountain Brigade on the date of 30 June 1991?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. After mobilisation, I responded to the call-up because I knew where my mobilisation post was in case there were wartime needs. I knew that it was the 216th Brigade, and I joined on the 30th of June. It was a Sunday. And I responded to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, first of all, ask you to slow down, Witness, because the interpreters missed the last part of your answer. You said: "... I joined on the 30th of June. It was a Sunday," and you responded to. And could you then repeat what you said. And you responded to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Responded to mobilisation call-up because there was a mobilisation of the army, the 216th Brigade, the 30th of June, and we had to respond to mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to look at me now. You should slow down in your speed of speech, otherwise your testimony will be lost. No one will be able to translate. So please slow down. Have you understood that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, just so you know, your statements have been admitted into evidence and -- so we move through faster here, if you could please not repeat information that's in your statement. I'm just asking very precise questions. If I need you to explain, I'll ask you to further explain. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of the statement that's been admitted as D532, you state that following the mobilisation, one battalion was sent to Banja Luka. Did you go to Banja Luka as a member of the 216th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were the operations commander of the 216th Mountain Brigade between 30 June 1991 and mid-May 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Ganic, who was now a general of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was then chief of operations of the 216th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you then please tell us what was your positions between 30 June 1991 and mid-May 1992 in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the 30th of June, I was assistant chief of operations to then-Major Ganic of the JNA. He's currently a general. He fled in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, whether he is now a general, whether he fled, what his family looks like, was not part of the question. You've answered the question by your first line, saying, "Well, from the 30th of June, I was assistant chief of operations to then-Major Ganic of the JNA." That's a full answer to the question. Would you refrain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from expanding on all kind of things you are not asked. Otherwise we will still be here at Christmas. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that you were the chief of operations from December 1991 to mid-May 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Once the VRS was formed, is it correct that you continued to serve as the chief of operations of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade between mid-May 1992 until the 19th of December 1994?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As an operations officer in the 1st Romanija Brigade, is it correct that you were directly subordinate to Dragomir Milosevic, who was the brigade commander until February 1993, and then Vlado Lizdek, the subsequent brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I was directly subordinated to the Chief of Staff. But the commander of the brigade was Dragomir Milosevic, and afterwards Vlado Lizdek.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As an operations officer at the brigade level, is it correct that you were familiar with the reporting procedures of the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part I was familiar, but I wasn't always the duty officer at the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Just -- I want to go through some of your previous testimony. In the Dragomir Milosevic case, at transcript page 5824, you described how the operations centre functioned in your brigade. You stated: "Each unit, a company, a platoon, a squad, a battalion, sent to the operations centre of the brigade, there are daily reports. And on the basis of those reports coming from battalions and brigade, the battalion and brigade drafted their reports and sent them to the corps command. We had radio communication and wire communications at the operations centres, and immediately the battalion commanders reported any provocation to the centre about what was happening on the separation line between the two armies -- or, rather, what kind of combat activity was in progress." Is it correct that this is how the operations centre of the 1st Romanija Brigade functioned?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it functioned. Except at the centre -- well, I wasn't there all the time. I was somewhere in the field or touring units, but I was there most of the time. I mean, there were always some officers at the brigade that were on duty, duty operations officers, day and night. And then that person would have to take notes, and then this person would report to me and to the commander and to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, at transcript page 5824 to 25, you further described the purpose of the reporting handled by the operations centre of your brigade. You were asked: "Q. And all that information that comes in and is collected in the operations centre is analysed on behalf of the commander of the brigade so he can make his decisions about how to proceed." You answered: "Yes. The commander of the brigade receives a report, and the duty operations officer and the operations and training organ prepare the regular combat reports to be sent to a higher command. These reports had to be approved by the brigade commander. In his absence, that would be the Chief of Staff. In his absence, though, this will have to be approved by an operations officer." Do you stand by this testimony? Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I fully stand by that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, at transcript page 5825, you further describe the type of reporting within the brigade. You were asked: "Q. Did you also orally brief the Chief of Staff or the brigade commander about what was happening in your area of responsibility, or is it only done by written reports?" You answered: "Both orally and in writing. Written reports were sent to higher ranking units, and the commander of the brigade received oral reports from the operations officer about the events involving the brigade." Is it correct that this statement of yours accurately describes both the oral and written reporting within your brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And whether it was oral or written reports, is it correct that it was the duty of the subordinate units to portray an accurate picture of what was happening in their areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They can send regular reports and interim reports during the day, but up until that day they have to send regular reports when the time is set for that. But they can send interim reports before that, too, if something is going on so that the command would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the brigades had to submit their daily written reports to the corps command by 2000 hours?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Coded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You read my mind. Is it correct that the SRK used coded references for locations, weaponry, and targets in its communications?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Ever SRK brigade had its own command post and forward command post; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Each of these command posts were staffed by duty officers; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: From the command posts, is it correct that the brigades could communicate with their subordinate battalions, the other brigades, or regiments in the corps and with the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: We could not communicate, but we knew who our neighbours were on the left and right. And if we were to communicate to ask for support, we'd have to send a request to a higher command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we're clear: From the command posts, you were able to communicate with your subordinate battalions and your superior SRK command; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were promoted and became an operations officer in the corps command of the SRK on 19 December 1994?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: More specifically, is it correct that you were an operations officer in the operations and training department of the corps command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were an operations officer in the corps command, is it correct that you were directly subordinate to Cedomir Sladoje, the SRK deputy commander and Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, directly to him. But the commander is the man in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. And at the time that you were at the corps command, that was Dragomir Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that there were a total of 10 to 11 operations officers in your department?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was, according to plan. But since we did not have enough personnel, there were only two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the corps operations centre was located at the Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Specifically, the operations centre was on the ground floor of the barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were at the SRK command, did the reporting between the brigade commands and the corps commander function in a similar manner as to when you were in the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In a similar way, that's how it was. But for the most part -- well, in writing. Sometimes orally, too. I mean, these reports. But actually requests were usually written from the brigade command to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the corps command sent daily reports to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Every day, yes. That was an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were the daily written reports from the respective brigades of the SRK also sent along with the corps command daily report to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they weren't. Just the corps command report would include all the brigades, so it was very well put together. Succinctly, clearly, precisely, what was happening in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and all brigades and all other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The daily dead-line for submitting reports from the SRK to the VRS Main Staff was 2100 hours; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. And sometimes there were interim combat reports, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These interim combat reports would be in addition to the daily combat report; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When necessary. Depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the offices of the corps commander, Dragomir Milosevic, and Cedo Sladoje, were located on the 1st floor of the Lukavica barracks; in other words, the floor above the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, except that one was on the left and the other one was on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Dragomir Milosevic and Cedo Sladoje used their offices as sleeping quarters?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You know this because you sometimes stayed around the clock in the operations centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were part of the corps command, is it correct that you would visit forward command posts in Trnovo, Nisici, and Vogosca with Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes by myself, and sometimes I was with the commander because usually the operations officer accompanies the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Whether it was by yourself or with the corps commander, how often would you go to the forward command posts during your time in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Vogosca, Nisici, and Trnovo. First I was there when there was this offensive attack -- in 1995, I was in Vogosca. And then I returned to Trnovo to the forward command post for the commander. I stayed there on my own. And in Vogosca, I was never on my own. Dragomir Milosevic was always there, and sometimes he'd come to Trnovo, too. First Cedo was there and then Cedo went back to the corps command, so Trnovo remained unmanned so then I manned that command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not quite sure I got an answer to the question I was asking. Are you able to approximate, just in terms of numbers, how often you would go to forward command posts during your time in the corps command? Once a week, once every two weeks, for months at times?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, when the offensive was on for 45 days, I was always at the command post. I was in Trnovo for 15 days, and then I was in Vogosca. Actually, the first 15 days in Vogosca, and then this last offence I was in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: And then from time to time I went, say, every five days, every ten days when there was no offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Milosevic case, at transcript page 5837, you described General Milosevic and his time in the field. You were asked: "Q. Now you just told us that you often accompanied General Milosevic during combat operations, and I believe also yesterday you said that General Milosevic was often in the field; is that correct?" You answered: "Yes, that's correct. That --"

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, let me finish --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You answered: "Yes, that's correct. That would be a real soldier, always on the front line, highly respected by the officers and soldiers alike, precisely because he was always there where the fighting was at its worst. He was not always just sitting in his office or where civilians were." Is it correct that this accurately describes your view of General Milosevic's presence in the field?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you consider Dragomir Milosevic to be a highly competent and educated officer?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Dragomir Milosevic held daily briefings with the SRK command staff in the morning, and then the SRK command staff would report back to General Milosevic in the evenings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, usually we'd have meetings in the morning. And then people were given tasks as to what they were supposed to do during the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the different assistant commanders from the different sectors that were part of the SRK command staff were all obligated to attend these detail meetings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unless they were absent due to well-founded reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Orders would be issued at these meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Marko Lugonja was the SRK assistant commander for security and intelligence while you were in the corps command; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Lugonja had two reporting chains, one that went directly to Dragomir Milosevic and the other that went to General Tolimir of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how security functions in every army in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would his reports to General Milosevic and General Tolimir both go through the operations centre in the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he reported to the commander every morning, as far as security is concerned. Sometimes he had these interim reports as well, and we wouldn't know about it because it's how security functions. And as far as his reports to Tolimir are concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please continue stating what you said after "... as far as his reports to Tolimir are concerned," was there something else that you added?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that I was not involved in security and intelligence because security is a different thing altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the security and intelligence department acted independent of the operations department?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't operate independently. They did have Tolimir as their chief. But that's how security functions. It is special in every army anywhere in the world, as I've already said. There is an assistant commander, Milosevic is in charge, but the intelligence -- intelligence service has its secret tasks, and not everybody can know about that. And perhaps they're following somebody in the command and even the commander wouldn't know about that. For example, they have their agents, Brzi [phoen] said that there would be an attack, et cetera. And Dragomir Milosevic would know who this Brzi is and then would let this person know. And then he's not supposed to know who this person is, but Lugonja and Tolimir probably know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that Tadija Manojlovic was the chief of artillery for the SRK?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Tadija Manojlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case, at transcript page 29237 to 38; you were asked to describe the link between SRK Artillery Chief Manojlovic and the VRS Main Staff. You stated: "Of course, he was linked with the chief of the artillery at the Main Staff. There are close links there. That is how the relations of subordination are in the army from top towards the bottom and from the bottom up in terms of reporting." Do you stand by this testimony as to say link between --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You said that there were close links there. Are you able to further describe the close links aside from the fact that there was reporting between Tadija Manojlovic and the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: If Tadija Manojlovic was the artillery chief in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, then it's normal that he closely co-operated with the Chief of the Main Staff, the deputy chief at the Main Staff for the artillery, and I co-operated with the operations organ at the Main Staff from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about Luka Dragicevic's interactions with General Gvero of the VRS Main Staff? How often would they meet and how did they co-ordinate their activities? So I'm asking about the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs at the corps level, and his relationship with his counterpart at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: General Dragicevic never submitted a report to me. He would submit a report to Commander Gvero, and then what was meant for me, I would be then told that because he was the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs, and -- which is a higher step up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you describe to us the co-ordination between SRK assistant commander for logistics, Aleksa Krsmanovic, and his counterpart in the Main Staff, General Djordje Djukic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that probably was connected. But I really didn't have anything much to do with that unless it was something that had to do with my own area of operations. In that case, I would be involved. He was the assistant commander. I wasn't his boss. He would not submit any reports to me, but I would report to him. But sometimes he would pass on certain information to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we are at break time. This is a good spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for a break. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes, and we'd like to see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 20 minutes past 1.00. I made a mistake, half past 1.00 we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, in the Karadzic case, at transcript page 29248, you were asked about meetings between the corps commander and the brigade commanders. You were asked: "The corps commander would also meet his brigade commanders as a group, wouldn't he?" You answered: "Yes. Very often the corps commander had briefings with the brigade commanders. But that was not that often. It was once a week or once in a fortnight." Can you confirm that this is your evidence with respect to the frequency of meetings between the SRK commander and the brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that General Milosevic's meetings with the brigade commanders were also attended by the commanders of the SRK's independent regiments that belonged to the corps, including the Mixed Artillery Regiment, or MAP, and the Mixed Anti-tank Regiment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you become the commander of the 4th Slpbr? When did you become commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of August, 1995. That's when I reported to the commander that I was ready, that the brigade is ready to carry out its combat assignments. I arrived a little bit before that in order to prepare to take over the battalions, to look over the support assets and logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that that was the same day in which the brigade was formed, the 7th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade was finally established on the 7th. As soon as the commander reports that the brigade is under his command, then it is considered as legally established and it begins to send out reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what Slpbr stands for.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That is the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you ever officially appointed? And when I say that, were you issued an official document that designated you as the commander of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was assigned to the post temporarily at first in writing. This was then extended and then the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I understand from your answer, then, that you received a temporary post which then was never actually made a permanent post because the war ended?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. This lasted for seven months or slightly longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I want to change topics now. So in your -- in paragraph 14 of your statement that's admitted as D532, you describe how the Trebevic Battalion, the Podgrab Battalion, and the Hresa Battalion were included as part of the 1st Romanija Brigade. You also explain how this expanded the brigade's zone of responsibility to include Mrkovici in the northern part of Sarajevo. Is it correct that this area in Mrkovici was previously held by the Hresa Battalion before it became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The Hresa Battalion became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade in 1992 and then it was no longer a part of it in 1994 and joined the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade. It was resubordinated to them. It became part of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. Two battalions were resubordinated to the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, and the Sokolovac, Trebevic, Jahorina, and Praca Battalions were left over. The 3rd and 4th went to the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I -- I appreciate what you're saying. However, before we get too far afield and with many other dates, I just want to try to go through this in a clear fashion focusing on certain time-periods. So what I asked you was before the Hresa Battalion became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade in 1992, did it hold the area of Mrkovici? Was that within its zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the area of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And that battalion also before it became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade held the feature known as Spicaste Stijene; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The name is Spicaste Stijene; somebody named it that way. But that name is not on that map. But it was held -- Mala Kula and the Spicaste Stijene. That's what the soldiers called that feature. It spread from Zecija Glava, including the village of Mrkovici excluding the village of Radoman, including Grdonj complex, seven [as interpreted], Suma, and a number of other features. This was the area that was held by the Hresa Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When the Trebevic, Podgrab, and Hresa Battalions became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade, is it correct that the brigade incorporated the weapons, vehicles, and equipment from these battalions as part of the brigade's assets?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, each battalion had its own assets. The brigade has its own assets when it needs to reinforce the battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when these battalions joined the 1st Romanija Brigade, they kept their own assets; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, have you dealt with Spicaste Stijene or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe the witness finally actually answered what I was looking for at the end of his answer on line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was whether you had dealt with that in a way or would you continue? Because I would have a question on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, go ahead. I was not going to return to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I read in your statement at paragraph 27 the following. You are quoted to have stated: "However, I can list a number of features in and around the city, such as Igman, Mojmilo, Debelo Brdo, Spicaste Stijene, Hum, Zuc, Grdonj, Bare, and others, which were dominant in relation to our lines of defence and from which they constantly shelled us and inflicted casualties, especially in Grbavica and Nedzarici." Now from one of your previous answers, I did not understand that Spicaste Stijene was held by the opposing party; whereas in your statement, it seems that you say it was held by the ABiH forces. Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Spicaste Stijene is located at the Grdonj feature. It was probably one or two forward trenches that were held by the Serbian army, and the flanks were held by the B and H Army, from the front and the left and right flank. And we were in Spicaste Stijene. But in the military topography, there is nowhere mentioned the name Spicaste Stijene. This is probably a name that was given to that feature by soldiers. But in the military topographical map, it's not noted anywhere by that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now if you say that you had some forward trenches there, and the Chamber has received quite some evidence about Spicaste Stijene, at least the number of features which dominated in relation to your lines of defence, would not be Spicaste Stijene in its entirety because parts of it were under Republika Srpska control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber. And, by the way, would the same be true -- Hum and Zuc, were they fully under the control of the opposing army, or was it partly held by the one army -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Republika Srpska held some parts to the east, and Hum and Zuc was part of a large feature, spreading from Kosevo all the way down to Sarajevsko Polje. Zuc is a large feature, it's a hill, and then any other hill or hillock has its own name. Each feature has its own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. But just to say that the features you listed in paragraph 27 were not all - and certainly not entirely - under the ABiH control. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit -- or, I'm sorry, 65 ter 30810.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, coming up before you will be a 5 November 1992 overview of weapons, vehicles, and other items from Commander Radislav Krstic who is of the 2nd Sarajevo -- or 2nd Romanija Mechanised Brigade to the SRK command and the 1st Romanija Brigade command. This document specifies the types of weapons and vehicles in the Trebevic, Podgrab, and Hresa Battalions. Is it correct that the 1st -- that these battalions were transferred from the 2nd Mechanised Brigade, Romanija Mechanised Brigade, to the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in September 1992. The Drina Corps was founded in October. And a part of the 2nd Romanija joined the Drina Corps, except these Pale battalions because, before that, they were part of the Sarajevo area, so it's normal for these battalions to be part of the Sarajevo Romanija Brigade. When Commander Galic came, that's what was done, and that's how this corps was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this document, on the page before you, we see an overview of weapons. On the first page that I think that you have on your screen, the weapons for the Trebevic Battalion and the Podgrab Battalion are listed. These are the weapons that remained within these battalions once they became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade; correct? And if you need to see the weapons for other battalions, I'd be happy to ask the Court Officer to continue to the next pages.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And is it correct that these were the weapons that remained within the battalions once they became part of the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they probably received additional weapons once they joined the SRK. Milosevic was there, and it was up to the commander to issue weapons. The Trebevic Battalion received some assets and reinforcements, like a self-propelled gun and a tank, a three-barreled gun as well, and a Praga and flak, which was an anti-aircraft machine-gun which used to be used on naval ships but it was mounted on a truck in this case. I don't know when it all happened exactly, but I know I had such assets in my brigade. I know that the 1st Romanija Brigade had them as well because I was familiar with it when touring the battalions. Now, as for where the commander received the weapons from and how those weapons were sent to the respective battalions, that is something I don't know. When I was there, there were even two 120-millimetre mortars as well as 82-millimetre and 60-millimetre mortars. But while they were in the 2nd Romanija unit, they did not have such 120-millimetre pieces. They didn't have the tank, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So I understand correctly, you say that two 120-millimetre mortars as well as 82 and I believe it's 60-millimetre mortars, these were added to the Trebevic Battalion once it joined the 1st Romanija Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Only the 120-millimetre pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't planning on going through all of them in detail. I've got the evidence I was seeking to elicit. I tender the document at this time, 65 ter 30810.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30810 receives number P6603, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, during your previous testimony in both the Milosevic and Karadzic cases, is it correct that you discussed the subject of modified air bombs possessed by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had testified to that effect in the case against General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Today I'm going to go through your previous testimony regarding modified air bombs in detail. But before doing so, I have one simple question: Is it correct that the modified air bombs possessed by the SRK were a completely inaccurate and highly destructive weapon?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not all brigades did have such launchers of air bombs. Five brigades did; two did not. I think the 1st Romanija did not have a launcher of air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to pause here just before going through your testimony so -- based on what you just mentioned. Could you list the five brigades that had modified air bomb launchers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: They are the Igman Brigade, the Ilidza Brigade, the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, the Ilijas Brigade, and perhaps the 2nd Brigade had it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "2nd Brigade," are you referring to the 2nd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it had such assets. I'm not sure. So the Ilidza, Igman, 3rd Sarajevo, and Ilijas Brigades did have it. I'm positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So we're clear: The Ilidza and Igman Brigades are located to the west of Sarajevo, and the 3rd Sarajevo and Ilijas Brigades are located to the north of Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case, at transcript page 29269 to 70, you were asked: "Q. And is it true with respect to modified air bombs that you often heard the commander saying they shouldn't be used because of your safety and because they weren't technically perfected?" You answered: "Well, yes. The air bombs with launchers were devised by craftsmen. They were not approved. They were not precise. And the elevation was determined based on the equipment on the lorry and the fuel that fuelled the air bombs, and that -- they could be off target by as much as 2 kilometres. That's why we were not supposed to use them in urban areas. We were allowed to use them only in wider areas where the two armies were in contact but there were no civilians, not in urban areas because there was a risk that we might actually hit our own men or civilians." Do you stand by this testimony today?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say you heard about modified air bombs from the commander, is it correct that you were referring to Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had to have known of the launchers in the brigades, and I did too. The launchers did not have rules of use, as would a rifle or a mortar have. That is why I considered them imprecise. They also did not have firing tables. They were probably borrowed from similar assets, such as multiple rocket launchers, but there was -- there were never any rules of use for such launchers or for air bombs. That is why I said that they had not been tested or approved. It was fuelled by rocket fuel. The engines were also not so reliable and could easily overshoot or undershoot. That is why they were imprecise. We wanted to target the exit of the Sarajevo tunnel, but we couldn't because UNPROFOR was at the airport. The tunnel was a very profitable military target because they used it for exit and entry, but we couldn't use the modified air bombs for the risk of hitting the tarmac, the runway. I don't know whether other targets were engaged, though. There was -- there were things in the Milosevic trial that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- such air bombs were used against Hrasnica, but I don't know about that. I was shown his order, which was not signed by him but by someone else. And I heard in the Karadzic trial that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- he agreed to it, although it was signed by someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I first again invite you to slow down. And, second, to just answer the question. The question simply was when you said you heard about modified air bombs, whether the commander, you said, had told you, whether that was Dragomir Milosevic. Was it him who told you about the modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the simple answer. We have now 15 or 20 lines of answer where a simple yes would have done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the use of modified air bombs had to be approved by the commander of the SRK, General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By the SRK commander. But he probably had to ask for approval from a senior command in order to be able to use such air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're again reading my mind with my next question. In turn, General Milosevic only authorised the use of modified air bombs with the approval of the VRS Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, you say that he probably had to ask for approval from a senior command. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. When I was the chief of operations, I presume he would have had to ask for Main Staff approval for the use of such air bombs. Perhaps even the ministry was involved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said after "perhaps the ministry was even involved," and then what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of Defence -- well, they had control over the factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just asking what you said. You were referring to the Ministry of Defence, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I just asked you to repeat what you said, not to start a new story. Listen to Mr. Weber's next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your previous answer in the Karadzic case, you stated that the modified air bombs could be off target by as much as 2 kilometres. Is it correct that this variance of as much as 2 kilometres was known throughout the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was known. But people also knew that it could be precise. It all depended on the engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did the SRK command inform the brigade commanders that these weapons could be off by as much as 2 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with any such orders, but I do know this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- when I testified in the Milosevic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry to cut you off, but I --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- I saw the order on the use of air bombs, and I said that it wasn't Milosevic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could listen to my questions, we'll go through this in a very orderly fashion. And if you're not familiar with something, that's fine. But if we could please proceed through this in an orderly fashion. In the Karadzic case at transcript page 29270, you were asked: "Q. And that's because, as you described them, they were completely inaccurate; correct?" You answered: "Completely inaccurate. They were not tested. Even some crews were killed and the commanders taken to court because it did happen that those bombs actually exploded there and then when they were activated. Only some of the brigades had them, not all of them. Only a few brigades on the strength of the corps had those air bombs, not all of them." Do you stand by this testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, are you still interested in an answer to one of your previous questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I missed it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question you have not answered, Witness, was: "Well, did the SRK command inform the brigade commanders that these weapons could be off by as much as 2 kilometres?" Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question for you. In view of the testimony just read to you and in view of your previous answers, I have some difficulties in understanding where you say that it was known that they could be 2 kilometres off "but people also knew that it could be precise. It all depended on the engines." Now, could you explain how the engines suddenly make the targeting by far -- more precise? That's what I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they fire earlier, it may overshoot or undershoot. It depended. Or it could go to the left or to the right, if one engine fired later than the other. So it all depended on whether all of the engines started at the same time. And even the Muslim side knew that no one could predict where such an air bomb would drop --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- despite of it being so destructive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, I understand that your testimony meant to be not that it could be more precise but that, depending on the engines, the projectile would fly further or shorter than in a situation where the engines would have functioned in a different way. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've mentioned a couple of times today that the modified air bombs were not tested. You also referred to the fact that there were no firing tables for the modified air bombs. Is it correct that there were no firing tables for the air bombs since there was no testing of them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I think. Because they were launched from trucks, and it was imprecise. They would choose elevations at random. I don't know how they decided on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say "they would choose elevations at random," are you referring to the SRK Commander Dragomir Milosevic and the brigade commanders or the artillery chiefs? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Artillery chiefs and the crews. They did it. It wasn't up to Dragomir Milosevic. He was not an expert in it. Now, whether they had some tables used for multiple rocket launchers, they may have. But I'm not familiar with how they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Dragomir Milosevic case, at transcript page 5801, you were asked: "Q. And you, yourself, did you hear any reports from other fighters from the other brigades about those air bombs?" You answered: "Yes, I did. I heard that some soldiers and some craftsmen were working on some make-shift launchers and this actually had not been done properly at all. You need to have a plane in order to drop an air bomb, and if you don't comply with the instructions for use with the manual, then you're not doing it properly, and you're incurring risk. I know that in one incident six of our soldiers were killed in this sector. This was imprecise, an imprecise weapon, and technically it was not perfected at all." Do you stand by this testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I do stand by what I said about its being technically imperfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you heard of some soldiers and craftsmen working on make-shift air bomb launchers in 1994?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that some craftsmen and engineers were working on it, but I don't know who exactly. Locksmiths and other craftsmen from the industry worked on it alongside engineers because the craftsmen alone --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- could not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I haven't asked you yet who. I was simply asking you when you heard some soldiers and craftsmen working on a modified air bomb launcher, was that in the year 1994?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it some time in 1993. Perhaps in the second half of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard it from the brigade commanders, those brigades which had them. It was the 2nd Romanija that had it, and then at Ilidza, and then at Igman where the repair institute was. They also had them at Vogosca, too. I could hear of such news from the commanders, soldiers, and artillery chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say the brigade commanders, and you mention Ilidza, is it correct that you heard about this from Vladimir Radicic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that he had a launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And he was one of the individuals that the SRK command had been -- had made aware that the modified air bomb could be off by as much as 2 kilometres; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: He was probably informed. He did test it, though. And he knows of it. He knows of one instance when it fell on his own positions but went unexploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm looking at the clock. We are one minute from --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Whenever is good for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have more questions on this topic, though, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Veljovic, we'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow morning 9.30 in the morning. We'd like to see you back. But -- no, don't take off your earphones yet. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or that is testimony still to be given. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is completely clear to me. This is the fourth time I am being told so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it becomes routine for you. You may follow the usher. That is perhaps routine as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 25th of June, in this same courtroom, I, 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of June, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25
